## The Invention of the internet: a military tool

In the year 1945, two things happened: World War 2 ended, and the term “Internet” was coined by the United States War Department. Although this term was originally meant to designate a network of radios, this term is now commonly used to refer to the World Wide Web, who didn’t come into existence until 1989 in the CERN (that’s us\!).

The US department of Defense originally funded ARPANET, more bureaucratically known as the **Advanced Research Projects Agency Network**

## The First Image boards:

Before talking about image boards, it is important to introduce their predecessor: textboards. Originating from Japan, they are simple websites, where one could be fully anonymous and start threads, similarly to how modern forums operate. Although this technology never really left Japan, it gave rise to Imageboards, the first one being Ayashii World, launched by Shiba Masayuki in 1996\. This gave rise to boards like Danbooru and the more influential Futaba Channel, colloquially known as ”2chan” in Japan, which, in 2003, inspired Christopher “Moot” Poole to make a very important board: **4Chan**.

## 4chan, the most (in)famous imageboard:

4chan is a weird website. I’ve personally never visited it as of August 2026 besides for the very famous “Story Time with a dead man” thread, which I won't touch on in this paper. Even though I highly recommend reading it if you’re interested in everything Epstein related.  
The thing that makes 4chan “a weird website”, is the sheer amount of THINGS you can find on there. The first screen one is greeted by when going on the website is a list of boards, as seen below:  
![][image1]

In my opinion, the most interesting boards are /b/, /pol/, /x/ and by far the weirdest /r9k/.  
/pol/ “politically incorrect”, /b/ “random” are 2 of the more chaotic and filled with some pretty disgusting people, who sometimes aren’t so bad, especially when animal cruelty is involved.  
/x/ is the “paranormal” board, which gave rise to a few things like the original foundation of creepypastas and more recently, the Backrooms.  
/r9k/ is hell. Plain and simple, it is filled with people who call themselves ROBOTs, because they are complete shut-ins, who have no employment, leeching off of their family, or unable to go outside due to mental or physical issues, hence the name r9k, signifying ROBOT9000 which is the algorithm used to moderate the board, where no 2 same posts are allowed to be posted. Wikipedia describes the board as “ *the origin of the "greentext" rhetorical style which often center around stories of social interactions and resulting ineptness.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4chan#cite_note-:5-39)[\[150\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4chan#cite_note-Morado-151) By 2012, personal confession stories of self-loathing, depression, and attempted suicide began to supersede /b/-style [roleplaying](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Role-playing_game), [otaku](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otaku), and video game discussion.[\[151\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4chan#cite_note-Contest-152)[\[152\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4chan#cite_note-PureInvention-153)* “

But that’s the worst of 4chan. Most of the website is filled with pretty normal people, who work normal jobs and “lurk” the website without really posting anything and just watching tha chaos happen, because the system that 4chan uses to promote posts or not is a brutal one: the sheer number of posts on the board means that if no interactions (comments) happen, the post is buried and becomes invisible. This is where the phrase commonly seen in comments “bump” originates. Back then, Facebook hadn’t made the “Like” button that we’re so used to, and people had to improvise, in their own way, to make it known that “I like this piece of content.”  
This style of quickness in lifetime paradoxically is what kept certain memes alive for so long. People liked familiarity and if something was recognizable, they’d bump it, and if it was too different, they didn’t give it the time of day. This is why memes in the long form era evolved in a linear fashion and not in a jumpy one like we see today. 

## An Example of 4chans’s dumb fun: The RickRoll

The “bait and switch” tactic has existed for as long as the hyperlink has existed on the internet. Let’s dive into how this bait and switch tactic gave us the infamous RickRoll.

For some context, Auto Moderation tools on forums have existed for a long time, but 4chan’s was special. Among other things, it replaced any instance of the string “egg” with “duck”, giving us the funny replacement “duckroll” when someone wanted to type “eggroll”. This made the funny people of 4chan think of making the image pictured below, the Duckroll.

The Duckroll became a meme bigger than anything related to eggrolls, and eventually started to be hidden in hyperlinks. And one time, someone decided to replace the duckroll link with the very famous youtube link for Rick Astley’s “Never Gonna Give You Up” Music video, and the rest is history. Here’s a short video that might expand your horizons if you’re interested: [documentary](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dQw4w9WgXcQ)

The Rickroll has survived for such a long time, that people now recognize the link, uniquely starting with a dQw, leading to a whole subgenre of youtube where people will reupload the song, so that it has a different link:

## YouTube Poop (YTP):

The origins of the term YouTube poop are obviously, from after YouTube was launched back on February 14th 2005, but surprisingly, the commonly agreed upon “first ever YTP” is an edited version of the The Adventures of Super Mario Bros. 3, a 1996 movie, edited into complete low-quality poop joke filled comedy gold.

This, and a trend of similarly badly edited (often with free software) videos made YTP pretty indicative of the atmosphere of the late 2000s and early 2010s: people would laugh at basically anything if it was loud, filled with comedic pauses and sometimes if it had a reversed audio or repeating jokes.

Interesting examples of how YTP was impactful specifically is that it inspired masterpieces like the MLG movement and it gave us legendary videos like “\[YTP\] Woody Loses his Schmoe” or “YouTube Poop: The Sky Had A Weegee”.

It is interesting to pose that by definition, YTP is always supposed to NOT be funny. The quality is supposed to be that of “poop” as if the whole video style was mere defecation coming out of YouTube’s behind.

It is also interesting to point out that the trend never really died, as we still see recent-ish videos like “\[YTP\] We Talked About Bruno” coming out in late 2021, parodying the now infamous “We don’t talk about bruno” song from “Encanto”, a song that was definitely making the rounds in that late 2021 period.

## LOLCATS: the first image macro trend:

In 2004, the term “image-macro” was coined by a user on the forum Something Awful. The term designated an image format in which it consists of an image with overlaid text. Usually, since these images were made using a website tool that lets you overlay text on stock images. This practice obviously made it to 4chan, a website that is built around images and funny captions.

Among all the other images that were used for image-macro purposes, one type prevailed as the all-time most popular: cat photos. To this day, having a cute cat on a meme is common, dare I say, the default, and pictured in the next section was debatably the most well-known cat-image-macro to have ever existed.

## The impact font:

The impact font takes its origins in the 1960s, designed by Geofferey Lee in 1965\. It was included in the “core fonts for the web” package included in Microsoft Windows since 98\.  
The big, thick letters of the font are meant to invoke an IMPACT in the reader, which gave it an unexpected use in the 2007 meme: icanhascheezburger seen below:

This gave rise, among other things, to [icanhascheezburger.com](http://icanhascheezburger.com), a blog-style website which included a built-in meme creator popularized the “TOP TEXT, BOTTOM TEXT” meme format, which exclusively used the impact font.

This style of early cat image with a cute caption captures perfectly the sort of dumb freedom the internet proposed, before governments and corporations realized that it had real power over the people. It lived in an age before ulterior motives and control as it clearly stated its intentions, to make people smile and laugh.

We’ll come back to this a bit later in section 5 to talk about how this, like many other memes, was taken into the hell of “post-post-post-post-irony”: the practice of adding layer after layer of irony to an image, where, at first, the meme itself is the thing people are laughing about, then, the meme is no longer funny, and then, in a contrarian kind of way, it is the fact that the meme is no longer funny that becomes funny, and then the cycle repeats. This is why grown people still say “nice” at the mere mention of the number 69, often forgetting the original meaning of the meme.

## Vine (2012)

Vine was founded in 2012 by three friends who met while working for another company: Dom Hofmann, Rus Yusupov, and Colin Kroll. It presented itself quite simply: an app that let you post looping, 6 second long videos for everyone to see.

The appeal of such a website was quickly seen by Twitter Inc. and it bought out the whole website before it even launched, for a lump sum of \$30 million.

Vine, to put it simply, was hugely successful. 2016 YouTube was filled with Vine compilations, and whole media personalities made their debut on Vine.  
Recognizable names like the Paul brothers, Jack Doherty and Zach King.

Vine’s UI decisions were quite genius. For example, competitors like Instagram and twitter had clunky tabs at the bottom, while Vine’s switcher was hidden on the home button at the top left. The concept that was quickly understood by the makers of Vine’s UI was that users like to stay on what they’re doing, and the tabs were just getting in the way.

The six-second duration was not chosen through obscure research or psychology, it was chosen through trial and error. They had actually tried other durations like 4,5,7 and even 10 seconds, and arrived at the 6 second duration as a nice in-between. 10 seconds made file sizes too big, and 5 seconds felt too short. The looping feature was actually done on accident, as they were trying to make the cutoff at the end of those 6 seconds a bit less anticlimactic. This loop feature was actually what made vine what it is, because it pushed the comedy on the platform to integrate the loop, making it so that a joke has to be heard 2 or 3 times to be understood, farming loops and watch time.

Due to the high supply of views, one would assume that vine would insert a built-in ad system, but, unlike the greedy corporate shareholders today, Vine’s execs thought that inserting pre or mid-roll ads onto 6 second videos would “absolutely destroy the user experience”. That meant that even if you had 100 million loops on a video, you made a crisp 0 dollars out of it. Because of this, users had to find other ways to monetize their creations, notably with product placement, where companies would pay anything in the range of 100\$ to 40000\$ per vine, depending on how many followers or how much reach users had.

To conclude, the reason why vine is important to internet culture is because it was quite literally the centre of human attention on the internet up until its demise, posting numbers as high as 200 million daily active users in December of 2015\.

## MLG: the spiritual successor to YTP (2013-2016)

## Minecraft: The World’s Biggest Video Game (2014)

I don’t think I need to introduce the concept of Minecraft to you, but I will as a formality and because I want this paper to be as accessible as possible to any and everyone. For this essay, talking about videogame icons like Minecraft is inevitable, because gaming is one of the biggest factors in internet culture, rivaling the likes of real world politics and other media like movies and TV shows.

In 2009, a demo for a game called “Cave Game” was posted onto a gamedev forum by Markus “Notch” Persson. At this point it’s still in its infancy, an era called “pre-classic”. This version of the game was pretty simplistic, being a cobblestone platform in the middle of the void with nothing to do except move with WASD, jump with space, look around with your mouse, right click to place a block of cobblestone and left click to break one. You could also press G to spawn a running player model, which would flail its arms around and eventually fall to its death in the infinite, empty void. This phase would last less than a week.

Later, we would get a small procedurally generated world, and a few more blocks and items, notably wood, trees and sand. This phase would be called classic, and the 

Later on, it would finally enter InfDev (infinity Dev), the stage of the game where you can kind of recognize the new name it would choose: MineCraft (later becoming Minecraft). At this point, you had tools, ores, procedural generation and fluids like water and lava. Many people started their journey here, and the game gained notoriety as quite the ambitious project.  
What interests us in this essay is mods. Game modification was pretty easy with Minecraft, ever since the forge abstraction layer let modders easily access minecraft’s code and, of course, with mods comes content, and with content, YouTube comes always shortly behind.  
Modded minecraft in 2014-15 was quite literally YouTube’s infinite money glitch. Many channels made names for themselves just by playing modded minecraft and impressing young children with huge mobs or obliteration rays. Among these creators, a few stand out: DanTDM, PopularMMOs and others amassed hundreds of millions of views in the matter of months. They quite literally were millionaires by playing kids games, and in PopularMMO’s case, by getting high or drunk and playing hyperstimulating lucky block survival.

In the greater modded minecraft genre, a few themes kept coming back: The Lucky Blocks mod, originally released on May 4th 2012 on Planet Minecraft, a forum still used to post mods, texture packs, data packs and more, presented a quite fun and simple premise: break lucky blocks, which had a mario-inspired Yellow Block with a white question mark texture, and either get lucky and have a good effect, like get diamonds or enchanted golden apples, or get unlucky and be trapped in a cage with an anvil falling high above you.

Another huge mod was OreSpawn, which has quite the history that I could write a whole other essay about, because its creator was quite the schizophrenic conspiracy nut. It was made by a dad to have fun with his kid, and obviously, it had some of what the kids considered cool as hell at that point: huge kaiju and big swords. 

All of this content, paired with the huge conventions that were held yearly: Minecon, cemented minecraft’s place in internet culture and in a way, started to live in everyone’s mind. Literally every single big YouTuber at the time was either talking about minecraft, playing minecraft or collabing with youtubers that played minecraft. It was simply the easiest way to ride the wave of popularity that led to 500 million copies being sold, the game being launched on the PS3, Xbox 360 and eventually even on phones, where it topped the app store and google play store in mere months.

## Commentary YouTube (2014)

YouTube is governed by an algorithm, one that either recommends your videos or doesn’t. The factors that determine whether or not a video pops off are measurable, and there are a few that are unalienable: consistency, and first hour viewtime. But, back in 2014, this was not the case. The only way to have success was to post every day, clickbait your viewers and retain their watch time for 10 whole minutes. That meant that if you didn’t upload for one day, you’d be dropped by the algorithm and you’d start at square 1\. Most of the pillars of commentary on youtube started by making MLG parodies, like Pyrocynical and Dolan Dark. LeafyisHere, a pretty big youtuber at the time, pivoted to commentary, and since at that point Pyrocynical was just copying Leafy, he’d soon follow suit and fully pivot into being a commentary YouTuber.

Commentary content in this era was surprisingly structured, and followed a few rules:

- CS:GO surf or Overwatch gameplay in the background (sometimes Garfield Kart if it was Pyrocynical)  
- Monotonous, deep (often fake) voice rambling about whatever internet personality you’re insulting today  
- Clickbait title to get them views  
- Almost exactly 10 minutes long to get midroll ads and make bank  
- Reacting to clips to pad out watch time

“Commentary” content was, of course, a stretch, because this content was mostly smearing other internet personalities or world events just to make money and get subscribers. The reason why they usually wouldn’t be under fire for insulting beloved or hated figures, is because these commentary youtubers would hide behind the excuse of “satire”.

The most important personality in this family of content is of course its pioneer: LeafyisHere. Calvin Lee Vail, better known as LeafyisHere began making commentary content in 2014, using the aforementioned CS:GO surf gameplay and reaction content, which would make him quite the figure. He quite literally exploded in popularity, going from 100’000 to 1’000’000 subscribers in a mere 6 months\!  
This popularity obviously led to many copycats, like pyrocynical, but also household names like KEEMSTAR, and iDubbz, which are now both infamous for their own reasons.

Leafy’s channel is now deleted, so i don’t really have access to his thumbnails, but archives exist and i have managed to recover a few indicative ones pictured here:

iDubbz is interesting because his “content cop” series is what most likely led to the death of the commentary genre, due to his excessive verbal violence and overall tone which lead to multiple controversies, ending with him completely leaving the internet, and never truly apologizing for what he did. iDubbz truly screwed every other commentary youtuber, because in his infamous video attacking leafy, he went too far, and YouTube had to change its harassment policies to ban him, and subsequently started to crack down on all of the unchecked harassment and cyberbullying that the commentary community was going through with.

## Fortnite, THE game. (2017)

Near the end of 2016, a trailer for an upcoming game was released onto youtube. The game was called Fortnite, and it was yet another Third person zombie survival game, with its main selling point being its expansive build system, where you could build anywhere on a general grid using one of three materials: wood, bricks and metal.

This “Save the world” mode that was about zombie survival, never really popped off. The real seller was the Battle Royale mode (100 players drop in different places, last one standing wins) that they introduced in 2017, riding the wave that Player Unknown’s BattleGrounds (PUBG) set, and ultimately, dominated the whole Battle Royale genre. They pioneered the Battle Pass system, where players would have a free pass, getting rewards for their playtime/level and a Premium Pass system where players would get extra cosmetics like skins, emotes and more, on a seasonal basis. Battle pass season 1 lasted 3 months, and every subsequent pass also lasted 3 months. The particularity that still exists in Fortnite’s Battle Pass is that buying enough v-bucks (the game’s premium currency, only purchasable with real money) for one battle pass would be all a player needed, because a battle pass paid for itself in rewards. Much like how Minecraft made household names in the 2015 era, Fortnite had a whole, bigger grip on the world, due to their emotes. Whereas minecraft needed art or visuals to be represented in the real world, fortnite had the advantage that it had recognizable dance moves that every kid knew on the playground and every kid could teach to other kids, adding a real-world layer of appeal to the game. Furthermore, back when i was a kid going through the fortnite boom, fortnite was one of the only games that had true, easy cross-platform compatibility. You could call up your friend who was on a PlayStation, Xbox, phone or PC and play without problem and pretty easily at that. Something that minecraft did not get until bedrock edition.

# IV: The Dark Ages: The Ad-pocalypse

## Political Extremism & Me, Context for the Ad-pocalypse: (2016)

Before we begin talking about political extremism, I'd like to preface the fact that this will most likely be one of the longer sections, so buckle up and be ready for some spew of internet lore that no one is ready for, ever.

Thinking back through it with the lens of a fully functioning adult by now, 2016 was really a crazy year, and 2017 even more so. Among other things, it’s the year I created my YouTube account and stopped using my mom’s one, and it’s when I had just gotten into 5P, cementing my place into the second cycle of primary school.

While I was still stuck between being at home and enjoying the wonders of Minecraft Let’s Plays and going out to play football with my friends, the internet was brewing something. And what it ended with, was the single darkest age it has ever seen.

We talked about 4chan in section 2 as an image board with quite lax rules on most of its boards, but to be honest, i’m quite scared of talking about that place because of its reputation as being quite literally the feeding ground for doxxers, C.H.U.D.s (self-proclaimed “Cannibalistic Humanoid Underground Dwellers”, better known as shut-ins or hikikomori)  
and the oh so mysterious “Anons” (anon being the short form of anonymous, which is the default name you get when signing up anonymously for the website). 

Among the shenanigans they may have partaken in over the many years that website has existed, one must understand that what they did in 2016 was simply unheard of. With their history of internet trolling mostly being “harmless” stuff like voting Kim Jong Un as Time’s “Person of the Year” using bots, or the many times they used geolocalisation data to find locations using photos to help in investigations, you wouldn’t really expect them to start any real, impactful problems.

But they did, and now we’re here, with the existence of Qanon and the Epstein files.

## Government Funded Political extremism: the rise of meme-bots

I want you, the reader of this essay, to put yourself in the shoes of an average teenager in 2016\. You watch vine compilations, look at your instagram feed regularly and maybe have a facebook account. You have a certain “tone” on the internet that is unique to the people of your age, and you have a severe distrust of institutions, because they are “cringe”, or because you know that they’re the one paying for ads to consciously change your mind on things. This is why, when you see an ad telling you to vote for a certain local candidate, you pay no mind, as you do with all other ads, your brain simply shuts off, as a sort of rejection for the parasite that is internet advertising.

This is exactly what the Internet Research Agency of Russia figured out around 2016\. People don’t listen to ads, they listen to their peers, or what they think are their peers.  
For that reason, Russia developed what people were calling the “Kremlin’s Troll Farm” where they would pose as regular people, posting memes and targeting specific people and demographics, particularly, the best example would be how they targeted the African-American community. Among other things, they would incite these people to "repeat patriotic and anti-immigrant slogans" and "elicit outrage with posts about liberal appeasement of 'others' at the expense of US citizens.", herein lies the image that was found on the website hosting the previous citation. It depicts an image that was hosted on one of the described “Troll accounts”, trying to influence voting of minorities, and in the failing case, these troll farms were used to increase mistrust in the 2016 election, trying to illegitimize it, or distract them from actually going to vote.

## The “official” start of the ad-pocalypse (2017):

On 11.01.2017, YouTube would change forever. PewDiePie, who had been the most subscribed channel on YouTube for a long while at that point, posted a video where he would react to and have fun with the website Fiverr, where you can pay anyone \$5 USD to do basically anything. Near the end of the video, he would make a decision that he, and many others would regret for him: he paid 2 sri lankan boys to hold up a sign with the words “DEATH TO ALL JEWS” inscribed on it, and shout “subscribe to KeemStar”, a rival youtuber known for his questionable takes. This would shine a light on how “unregulated” YouTube was, and it would make the English times pull their ads from youtube after seeing them next to ISIS and neo-nazi videos.

## December 2017: The serious lapse in Logan’s Judgement:

In December of 2017, Logan Paul, which we will talk about more in depth in the next section, would film a video in the Aokigahara forest in japan, a notorious suicide spot, where, during the video, the famous line “guys… I think he’s dead” would be uttered in front of a dead corpse of a recently suicided man.The video would get Logan into so much hot water that he would be permanently banned from ever going to ASIA and prompted him to make one of the worst apology videos of all time, beginning with the infamous phrase: "I have made a serious and continuous lapse in my judgement”. Coupled with the crocodile tears in this video, one does not need to be a genius to predict that the internet was absolutely LIVID, to a point where mainstream media caught onto it, making many companies who had, as recently as one month before the video coming out, put their ads back on the platform, pull out once again, bleeding youtube’s money and making the ad-austerity even worse, plunging youtube into an even bigger hole of mainstream mistrust, which, writing this down today, in 2026 when you can scroll instagram and find child human sex trafficking rings being ADVERTISED on fresh accounts is absolutely insane.

This, among other things, would cause the ad-pocalypse’s second wave: the raising of partner program eligibility requirements. Partners now had to have 10000 subscribers and 4000 watch hours yearly, which, for smaller, nicher creators, was definitely a struggle.

To picture this, imagine a small creator who makes videos about woodworking and carpentry. If this creator were to have a piece that would blow up on another platform like facebook or instagram, many people would go subscribe to him, and before the second wave of apocalyptic destruction, this would be fine, because he’d still be eligible for the partner program on the amount of flat views he got alone. Post second wave ad-pocalypse, this would not be enough, because he wouldn’t be meeting the quite monstrous 4000 hour yearly watch hour requirement.

# V: The Modern Times

## THE PAUL BROTHERS: BEELZEBUB AND SATAN (2018)

The Paul brothers, better known as Jake Paul and Logan Paul, are more than just influencers these days. They have boxing careers, crypto scam experience and even ties to the President of the United States of America.

But back in the olden days of Vine, these two brothers were freshly adults, being 23 and 21 in 2018, absolutely dominated the site, and decided to move  to youtube, dominating said site too. Their reign was so absolute, it had whole divisions brewing in playgrounds all around the world, placing kids either in Team 10, the Jake faction, or the Mavericks, Logan’s Faction. Their kid-targetted, money-splurging luxurious lifestyle videos where they would jump on cars, spend outrageous amounts of money on food, beverages or parties would hook young viewers effortlessly, raking in free watch time and since they were technically Family-Friendly channels, the ad-pocalyptic ad policies wouldn’t affect them.

Offshoot channels, which tried to ride on their glory were people like Morgz in the UK, promoting similar styles of money-splurge “i spent \$10000 on XYZ” videos which would, in simple terms make absolute BANK, far outperforming the initial investment.

Social Blade showed channels like Logan and Jake Paul would make around \$200’000/month, which really switched the way of thinking about youtube. The sentiment around social media had already started to brew at this point, but now it was unavoidable. With family-friendly content farms making over 6 digits of revenue per year, YouTube was no longer a simple video-hosting site, but an actual career option.

## Minecraft Mondays (2019):

This is my essay, so i’m bound to talk about my favourite thing to ever happen post-adpocalypse: Minecraft Monday.  
Back in the day, Minecraft was seen as a kids game and had kind of died.   
But, in 2019, PewDiePie, the most subscribed channel on YouTube at the time, would start his minecraft series, reviving the game single handedly. This led to minecraft mondays, a weekly streaming event where youtubers of every caliber, minecraft or not, would play hunger games every Monday to gain points, and the winner at the end would get 100’000 dollars. This gave rise to the terrifying reign of Technoblade.  
Technoblade was a Skywars/Bedwars YouTuber for the longest time, his specialty would be his insane skill for Player versus Player combat on minecraft for the whole lifetime of his channel, originally playing hunger games on hypixel, and moving to the aforementioned other PvP gamemodes later on, skywars and bedwars.  
To put it simply, Technoblade was by far the most skilled player in the event, and it wasn’t close. he would amass 2x the amount of points of second place, and place himself at the top of the community, gaining a huge following and making a name for himself, getting a custom prefix on the game’s biggest server, the exclusive \[PIG+++\] rank on hypixel.  
These events were not only a huge popularity boost for this youtuber, but they were also some of the most fun one could have during the COVID lockdowns, because you couldn't go outside.

## the COPPA act (2019):

The COPPA act was an act of the Federal Communication Commission of the USA to protect children from abusive targeted advertising on TV. This rule however, legally was to be enforced onto youtube, and yet they didn’t. Landing them a fine of 130 million dollars and a hefty lawsuit nicely asking them to change their child protection policies

# VI: The TikTok Age

## What on earth is a TikTok? (2019)

TikTok, formerly known as [Musical.ly](http://Musical.ly) before ByteDance bought it out for \$3million in 2019, was, in its [musical.ly](http://musical.ly) days still a lip-syncing/dancing platform which wasn’t specifically popular, but not particularly unpopular either. The change that would propulse TikTok to popularity in 2021 would be its state-of-the-art chinese ultra-mega-addiction-dopamine algorithm, that, coupled with the fact that no video could surpass 1 minute in length, and that the concept of scrolling was pioneered there,  would hijack dopamine receptors into scrolling endlessly. The worst part of it is how it would rope kids into it, because no kid had ever received so much dopamine for so little effort.

# VII: AI, the far future

## What is SLOP?

Originally derived from the term “goyslop”, a term used in anti-semitic circles such as /b/ to designate low-quality food that jewish people would supposedly feed the goyim (non-jews) to prevent them from having quality offspring and develop to overthrow their jewish masters.  
It also is derived from the original word “slop”, which can be used to describe anything that is disgusting and low-quality, such as military food, corpses etc…   
The suffix \-slop was coined in 2023 mostly by pyrocynical’s fanbase. Pyrocynical is one of the many commentary YouTubers who made his name during that boom talked about in the “Golden Age” section.  
These days, the suffix is used to signify the lack of quality of something: “friendslop” being a video game that you buy once, to play with your friends once and never touch again (games like PEAK, R.E.P.O. and Lethal company), slop channels, which, in pyro’s case refers to his second channel, PyroLIVE, where he posts low-effort reaction content to fund his bigger projects on the main channel. The most common modern use of the term slop though, and the one recognized as the main signification, is the condensated form of “AI slop” meaning low-effort, AI-generated content, usually farmed for views on Youtube Shorts or Youtube Kids.
